events.name: New Year (Shogatsu)
events.recurrence_note: Annual public holiday period centered on January 1, with many businesses extending closures through January 3.
events.date_note: January 1 is the national holiday; practical closures often run longer.
events.traveler_summary: Japan's New Year period is family-centered and can affect restaurants, shops, museums, and transport patterns.
events.cultural_context: Many people visit shrines and temples for hatsumode, the first visit of the year, and spend time with family.
practical_guidance: Book intercity rail and hotels early if traveling around the holiday period.
Check restaurant, museum, and attraction hours directly because closures vary.
Expect shrine and temple areas to be busy and follow posted queueing instructions.
etiquette_notes: Move slowly and respectfully at shrine and temple queues.
Avoid blocking worship areas for photos.
Follow local instructions for purification, offerings, and no-photo zones.

events.name: Golden Week
events.recurrence_note: Annual cluster of national holidays from late April into early May.
events.date_note: Exact long-weekend pattern changes by year.
events.traveler_summary: Golden Week is one of Japan's busiest domestic travel periods and can strain hotels, trains, highways, and popular attractions.
events.cultural_context: Multiple national holidays fall close together, creating a peak period for domestic leisure travel.
practical_guidance: Reserve hotels, restaurants, and long-distance rail as early as possible.
Avoid same-day assumptions for popular attractions and transport.
Build extra buffer time around major stations and intercity moves.
etiquette_notes: Queue patiently at stations, elevators, and attractions.
Keep luggage compact on crowded trains where possible.

events.name: Obon
events.recurrence_note: Annual Buddhist observance usually marked in mid-August in many regions, with regional variation.
events.date_note: Dates vary by region and family tradition.
events.traveler_summary: Obon can create heavy domestic travel as people return to family homes and visit ancestral graves.
events.cultural_context: The observance honors ancestors and is often tied to family gatherings, memorial visits, and local festivals.
practical_guidance: Expect crowded trains, domestic flights, and highways around the main holiday window.
Check local festival schedules because some neighborhoods host evening dances or events.
Treat cemeteries, temples, and memorial spaces quietly and respectfully.
etiquette_notes: Do not interrupt private family observances for photos.
Keep voices low around temples, graves, and memorial areas.

events.name: Sanja Matsuri
events.recurrence_note: Usually held over a weekend in May in Asakusa.
events.date_note: Confirm exact dates each year with official Tokyo event listings.
events.traveler_summary: Sanja Matsuri brings major crowds to Asakusa around Senso-ji and Asakusa Shrine.
events.cultural_context: The festival is a major Tokyo shrine festival with mikoshi processions and dense neighborhood participation.
practical_guidance: Use nearby stations flexibly and expect crowd controls.
Avoid stepping into procession routes unless directed.
Keep bags close and leave extra time for movement around Asakusa.
etiquette_notes: Do not touch festival objects or join carrying groups unless invited.
Follow police, station staff, and event marshal instructions.

sensitivity_notes.title: Shrine and Temple Etiquette
sensitivity_notes.traveler_summary: Shrines and temples are active religious and cultural spaces, even when they are also major tourist sites.
sensitivity_notes.why_it_matters: Quiet behavior, respectful photography, and attention to posted rules help travelers avoid accidental disrespect.
avoid: Photographing interiors, ceremonies, or worshippers where signs restrict it.
Touching ritual objects, ropes, gates, or offerings casually.
practical_safe_behavior: Follow posted photo rules and staff directions.
Step aside after taking photos so worshippers can pass.
Keep voices low and treat queues as part of the visit.
examples: At a crowded New Year shrine visit, take photos from the side rather than from the front of the prayer area.
At temples with no-photo signs inside halls, keep the camera away even if other visitors ignore the sign.

sensitivity_notes.title: Quiet Public Conduct and Queueing
sensitivity_notes.traveler_summary: Public transport, shops, elevators, and attractions often rely on quiet voices and orderly queueing.
sensitivity_notes.why_it_matters: Loud calls, blocking paths, or pushing into queues can create friction quickly in crowded settings.
avoid: Taking phone calls in quiet train cars.
Stopping suddenly in station walkways to check maps.
Cutting queues or spreading luggage across seats.
practical_safe_behavior: Step to the side before checking directions.
Queue where locals are queueing and follow floor markings.
Use a low voice on trains, buses, and in small restaurants.
examples: At a busy Tokyo station, move near a pillar or wall before reviewing directions.
On trains, use messaging rather than speakerphone or loud calls.

sensitivity_notes.title: War Memory and Memorial Sites
sensitivity_notes.traveler_summary: Memorials, museums, and sites connected to wartime history should be approached with a calm and respectful tone.
sensitivity_notes.why_it_matters: These places may hold personal, national, and international meaning for visitors and local communities.
avoid: Making jokes, staged poses, or casual content at memorials.
Arguing with staff or visitors about historical interpretation in solemn spaces.
Filming grieving visitors or private ceremonies.
practical_safe_behavior: Read posted guidance before photographing or recording.
Keep discussion measured and move sensitive conversations away from memorial areas.
Use official museum context when summarizing what you learned.
examples: At a peace memorial, keep videos informational rather than performative.
If a group is holding a ceremony, give them space and do not film faces without consent.

sensitivity_notes.title: National Symbols and Local Pride
sensitivity_notes.traveler_summary: Treat flags, ceremonies, local traditions, and regional identity markers with basic respect.
sensitivity_notes.why_it_matters: Respectful behavior around national and local symbols helps travelers avoid unnecessary offense.
avoid: Using flags, monuments, or ceremonial spaces as comedy props.
Mocking local mascots, rituals, uniforms, or formal events in public content.
Ignoring staff instructions during ceremonies or formal visits.
practical_safe_behavior: Observe quietly before photographing formal events.
Ask permission before filming people in traditional dress or uniforms.
Keep social posts factual and respectful.
examples: At a local festival, photograph the procession without stepping into the route.
At a public ceremony, wait until others move before leaving or filming.
